questions.assertion: When a pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure short pea plant (tt), all the F1 plants are tall.
questions.reason: A single copy of the factor T is enough to make a pea plant tall.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: every F1 plant is Tt, and because T is dominant one copy of it makes the plant tall; the recessive t is inherited but not expressed.

questions.assertion: In human beings, the sex of a child is decided by the chromosome it inherits from its mother.
questions.reason: A woman has a perfect pair of sex chromosomes, both of which are X.
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: A is false: every child gets an X from the mother, so the mother cannot decide the sex; it is decided by whether the father passes on an X (girl) or a Y (boy). R is true: women are XX.

questions.stem: Plants in a field of sugarcane show very little variation, while human beings show quite distinct variations among individuals. Give the reason for this difference.
questions.answer: Sugarcane is raised by asexual (vegetative) propagation, so the new plants carry copies of the same DNA; variation arises only from small inaccuracies in DNA copying. Human beings reproduce sexually: each child receives DNA from two different parents, so new combinations are produced and much greater diversity results.
valuePoints: Sugarcane reproduces asexually, so variation comes only from minor inaccuracies in DNA copying
Humans reproduce sexually; combining DNA from two parents creates far greater variation

rubric.label: Sugarcane
rubric.descriptor: Asexual/vegetative propagation; only small DNA-copying errors give variation

rubric.label: Human beings
rubric.descriptor: Sexual reproduction combines DNA of two parents, giving more variation

questions.stem: Explain, using the example of plant height, how a gene controls a characteristic of an organism.
questions.answer: A gene is a section of DNA that provides information for making one protein. Plant height depends on the amount of a growth hormone, which is made by a process that depends on an enzyme (a protein). If the gene makes an efficient enzyme, a lot of hormone is made and the plant is tall; if the gene has an alteration that makes the enzyme less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is short.
valuePoints: A gene is a section of DNA carrying information for one protein (here an enzyme)
The efficiency of the enzyme decides how much growth hormone is made, and so whether the plant is tall or short

rubric.label: Gene to protein
rubric.descriptor: Gene = DNA section that codes for a protein/enzyme

rubric.label: Protein to trait
rubric.descriptor: Efficient enzyme → more hormone → tall; less efficient → less hormone → short

questions.stem: Tall F1 pea plants (Tt) are self-pollinated and 800 plants are obtained in the F2 generation. How many of these are expected to be short? How many are expected to be tall plants of the genetic make-up TT?
questions.answer: Tt × Tt gives TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1. Short plants (tt) = ¼ × 800 = 200. Tall plants that are TT = ¼ × 800 = 200 (the remaining 400 tall plants are Tt).
valuePoints: F2 ratio TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1
200 short (tt) plants
200 tall plants are TT

rubric.label: Ratio
rubric.descriptor: States 1 : 2 : 1 (or 3 tall : 1 short with ¼ TT)

rubric.label: Numbers
rubric.descriptor: 200 short; 200 TT (½ mark each)

questions.stem: A pea plant with round, green seeds (RRyy) is crossed with a pea plant with wrinkled, yellow seeds (rrYY). (a) What will the F1 plants look like, and what is their genetic make-up? (b) Name the kinds of germ cells the F1 plants can form. (c) State the ratio of seed types expected in the F2 generation, and name the new combinations that appear.
questions.answer: (a) All F1 seeds are round and yellow; genetic make-up RrYy. (b) RY, Ry, rY and ry. (c) Round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Round yellow and wrinkled green are new combinations not present in either parent, which shows that seed shape and seed colour are inherited independently.
valuePoints: F1 round, yellow; RrYy
Four kinds of germ cells: RY, Ry, rY, ry
F2 ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 with new combinations round yellow and wrinkled green

rubric.label: F1
rubric.descriptor: Round yellow and RrYy

rubric.label: Germ cells
rubric.descriptor: All four: RY, Ry, rY, ry

rubric.label: F2 ratio and new combinations
rubric.descriptor: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (½) and names the new combinations (½)

questions.stem: Explain how the sex of a child is determined in human beings. Why is the chance of having a boy or a girl equal?
questions.answer: Human beings have 22 pairs of chromosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes. Women are XX and men are XY. Every egg carries an X. Half the sperms carry an X and half carry a Y. If a sperm carrying X fertilises the egg, the child is XX, a girl; if a sperm carrying Y fertilises it, the child is XY, a boy. Since X- and Y-carrying sperms are formed in equal numbers, the chance of a boy or a girl is equal, and the sex is decided by what the child inherits from the father.
valuePoints: Women XX, men XY
Egg always carries X; sperm carries X or Y in equal numbers
X from father → girl, Y from father → boy; so equal chance

rubric.label: Sex chromosomes
rubric.descriptor: Women XX, men XY

rubric.label: Gametes
rubric.descriptor: All eggs X; sperms half X, half Y

rubric.label: Outcome
rubric.descriptor: XX girl, XY boy; father's chromosome decides; 50 : 50 chance

questions.stem: A tall pea plant with round seeds is crossed with a short pea plant with wrinkled seeds (ttrr). All the progeny are tall, but about half of them have round seeds and half have wrinkled seeds. Work out the genetic make-up of the tall parent and explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The tall parent is TTRr. Height: every progeny is tall, so each must receive a T from the tall parent; the tall parent therefore has no t to pass on and is TT (the short parent gives t, so all progeny are Tt and tall). Seed shape: the wrinkled parent can give only r. Half the progeny are wrinkled (rr), so half the germ cells of the tall parent carry r; half the progeny are round (Rr), so the other half carry R. Hence it is Rr. Genetic make-up: TTRr.
valuePoints: All progeny tall → tall parent TT
Half wrinkled → tall parent carries r as well as R, i.e. Rr
Answer TTRr

rubric.label: Height
rubric.descriptor: Reasons that all-tall progeny means the tall parent is TT

rubric.label: Seed shape
rubric.descriptor: Reasons that a 1 : 1 round : wrinkled split means Rr

rubric.label: Answer
rubric.descriptor: TTRr

questions.stem: Describe Mendel's experiment in which a tall pea plant was crossed with a short pea plant and the progeny were studied over two generations. Show the cross using the symbols T and t, give the ratios obtained in the F2 generation, and state what these results tell us. How could we confirm that the F2 generation really has TT, Tt and tt plants in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1?
questions.answer: Parents: pure tall TT × pure short tt. Germ cells T and t; F1 all Tt, and all F1 plants are tall — no medium-height plants, so only one parental trait is seen. F1 plants are self-pollinated: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. F2 genotype ratio TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1; phenotype ratio tall : short = 3 : 1, i.e. one quarter are short. Conclusions: the shortness trait was inherited by the F1 plants but not expressed, so there are two copies of the factor (gene) for each trait; T is dominant and t recessive; the factors separate when germ cells form and come together again at fertilisation. To confirm 1 : 2 : 1, self-pollinate each F2 tall plant and grow its progeny: about one-third of the tall plants (TT) give only tall progeny, while two-thirds (Tt) give tall and short progeny in the ratio 3 : 1; the short F2 plants (tt) give only short progeny.
valuePoints: TT × tt → F1 all Tt, all tall, no intermediate
F1 selfed → F2 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; 3 tall : 1 short
Two copies of each factor; T dominant, t recessive; recessive trait carried but not expressed in F1
Confirmation: self-pollinate F2 tall plants — one-third breed true, two-thirds give 3 : 1

rubric.label: F1 cross
rubric.descriptor: TT × tt, gametes, F1 all Tt and tall

rubric.label: F2 cross
rubric.descriptor: Tt × Tt worked, giving TT, Tt, Tt, tt

rubric.label: Ratios
rubric.descriptor: 1 : 2 : 1 genotype and 3 : 1 phenotype

rubric.label: Conclusions
rubric.descriptor: Two copies of factor; dominant/recessive; recessive hidden in F1

rubric.label: Confirmation test
rubric.descriptor: Self-pollinating F2 tall plants: ⅓ breed true, ⅔ give 3 : 1

questions.stem: (a) Explain how variations accumulate over succeeding generations when a single organism reproduces asexually. (b) Why does sexual reproduction produce much greater diversity, and how is the equal genetic contribution of both parents ensured? (c) Do all variations have an equal chance of surviving? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: (a) An organism gives rise to individuals similar in body design but with subtle differences caused by small inaccuracies in DNA copying. When these individuals reproduce, the next generation inherits the differences of their parents and also gets newly created ones, so differences build up generation after generation. (b) In sexual reproduction each parent contributes practically equal amounts of genetic material, so every trait can be influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA and new combinations arise. Genes are present on separate chromosomes; each cell has two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Each germ cell takes one chromosome from each pair (of either maternal or paternal origin), so it has one set; when a male and a female germ cell fuse, the normal number is restored with one set from each parent. (c) No. Depending on the nature of the variation, individuals get different advantages; for example, bacteria that can withstand heat will survive better in a heat wave. Selection of variants by environmental factors is the basis of evolutionary processes.
valuePoints: Asexual: small DNA-copying errors; differences inherited and new ones added each generation
Sexual: DNA from two parents gives new combinations and greater diversity
Each germ cell carries one chromosome of each pair; fusion restores the number, one set from each parent
Variations differ in survival value — heat-tolerant bacteria in a heat wave

rubric.label: Accumulation in asexual reproduction
rubric.descriptor: Minor DNA-copying inaccuracies; inherited differences plus new ones each generation

rubric.label: Greater diversity in sexual reproduction
rubric.descriptor: Both parents contribute DNA, producing new combinations

rubric.label: Equal contribution
rubric.descriptor: Two copies of each chromosome; germ cell takes one from each pair; fusion restores the number

rubric.label: Survival of variants
rubric.descriptor: Not equal; example such as heat-resistant bacteria

questions.passage: In a science club meeting, students compared how different animals decide whether a young one will be male or female. One group found that in a few reptiles the temperature at which the fertilised eggs are kept decides the sex. Another group reported that in snails an individual can change its sex. A third group studied human beings, in whom 22 pairs of chromosomes have one maternal and one paternal copy, and one further pair, the sex chromosomes, is not always a perfect pair. They drew a chart showing the sex chromosomes of a mother and a father and of the possible children.

parts.prompt: In which of the following is sex NOT genetically determined, according to the club's findings?
parts.answer: (b) — snails can change sex, which shows that their sex is not genetically determined.

parts.prompt: Write the sex chromosomes of a human male and a human female.
A couple already has two daughters. A relative says their third child is more likely to be a boy. Is this correct? Explain.
parts.answer: No. For every child the mother gives an X, and the father's sperm is equally likely to carry an X or a Y, so each child has an equal (1 in 2) chance of being a boy or a girl, whatever the earlier children were. (1 mark: equal chance for each child; 1 mark: reason — father's X or Y sperm in equal numbers, each birth independent)

questions.assertion: Concave mirrors are commonly used as shaving mirrors.
questions.reason: The focal length of a spherical mirror of small aperture is half its radius of curvature.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A concave mirror is used for shaving because, with the face held between the pole and the focus, it forms an erect, enlarged image of the face.

questions.assertion: A ray of light travelling obliquely from air into glass bends towards the normal.
questions.reason: Light travels faster in glass than in air.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down in glass, and that is why it bends towards the normal.

questions.stem: State the two laws of reflection of light. A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
questions.answer: (i) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (ii) The incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. Angle of reflection = 35°, so the angle between the incident and reflected rays = 35° + 35° = 70°.
valuePoints: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane
Angle between the rays = 70°

rubric.label: Laws
rubric.descriptor: Both laws stated (½ each)

rubric.label: Angle
rubric.descriptor: 70° with reasoning

questions.stem: Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 25 cm. If it is placed in contact with a convex lens of power +6 D, find the power of the combination and state whether the combination is converging or diverging.
questions.answer: Concave lens: f = −25 cm = −0.25 m, so P = 1/f = 1/(−0.25 m) = −4 D. Combination: P = P₁ + P₂ = −4 D + 6 D = +2 D. The power is positive, so the combination is converging (f = 1/2 m = 50 cm).
valuePoints: P of concave lens = −4 D (f in metres, negative sign)
Net power = +2 D, converging

rubric.label: Power of concave lens
rubric.descriptor: −4 D with the negative sign; ½ if sign or conversion wrong

rubric.label: Combination
rubric.descriptor: +2 D (½) and converging (½)

questions.stem: The refractive index of water is 1.33 and that of crown glass is 1.52. Taking the speed of light in air as 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, find (a) the speed of light in water, and (b) the refractive index of crown glass with respect to water.
questions.answer: (a) n = c/v, so v = c/n = (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/1.33 ≈ 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (b) n(glass w.r.t. water) = v(water)/v(glass) = n(glass)/n(water) = 1.52/1.33 ≈ 1.14.
valuePoints: Relative refractive index = 1.52/1.33 ≈ 1.14

rubric.label: Speed in water
rubric.descriptor: ≈ 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ with unit

questions.stem: An object 3 cm high is placed 18 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 24 cm. Using the New Cartesian Sign Convention, find the position, size and nature of the image.
questions.answer: R = −24 cm, so f = R/2 = −12 cm; u = −18 cm. Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, so 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/12 + 1/18 = (−3 + 2)/36 = −1/36, v = −36 cm. The image is 36 cm in front of the mirror. m = −v/u = −(−36)/(−18) = −2, so h′ = m × h = −2 × 3 cm = −6 cm. The image is real, inverted and magnified (6 cm high).
valuePoints: f = −12 cm, u = −18 cm with signs
v = −36 cm (in front of mirror)
m = −2, h′ = −6 cm; real, inverted, enlarged

rubric.label: Signs and formula
rubric.descriptor: f = −12 cm, u = −18 cm, mirror formula written

rubric.label: Image distance
rubric.descriptor: v = −36 cm

rubric.label: Size and nature
rubric.descriptor: h′ = −6 cm (½); real, inverted, magnified (½)

questions.stem: For a convex lens, state the position, relative size and nature of the image when the object is placed (a) at infinity, (b) beyond 2F₁, and (c) between F₁ and the optical centre O.
questions.answer: (a) Object at infinity: image at the focus F₂, highly diminished (point-sized), real and inverted. (b) Object beyond 2F₁: image between F₂ and 2F₂, diminished, real and inverted. (c) Object between F₁ and O: image on the same side of the lens as the object, enlarged, virtual and erect.
valuePoints: At infinity: at F₂, point-sized, real, inverted
Beyond 2F₁: between F₂ and 2F₂, diminished, real, inverted
Between F₁ and O: same side as object, enlarged, virtual, erect

rubric.label: Object at infinity
rubric.descriptor: Position, size and nature all correct

rubric.label: Object beyond 2F1
rubric.descriptor: Position, size and nature all correct

rubric.label: Object between F1 and O
rubric.descriptor: Position, size and nature all correct

questions.stem: A convex mirror used as a rear-view mirror on a scooter has a radius of curvature of 2.0 m. A car is 4.0 m behind the mirror. Find the position of the image of the car and the magnification, and state the nature of the image.
questions.answer: R = +2.0 m, so f = +1.0 m; u = −4.0 m. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/1.0 + 1/4.0 = 1.25 m⁻¹, so v = +0.8 m: the image is 0.8 m behind the mirror. m = −v/u = −(0.8)/(−4.0) = +0.2. The image is virtual, erect and diminished (one-fifth the size of the car).
valuePoints: v = +0.8 m behind the mirror
m = +0.2; virtual, erect, diminished

rubric.label: Signs
rubric.descriptor: f = +1.0 m (from R/2) and u = −4.0 m

rubric.label: Image position
rubric.descriptor: v = +0.8 m, behind the mirror

rubric.label: Magnification and nature
rubric.descriptor: m = +0.2 (½); virtual, erect, diminished (½)

questions.stem: Describe the position, size and nature of the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed (i) at infinity, (ii) beyond C, (iii) at C, (iv) between C and F, and (v) between P and F. Give one use of a concave mirror that depends on case (v).
questions.answer: (i) At infinity: image at F, highly diminished (point-sized), real and inverted. (ii) Beyond C: image between F and C, diminished, real and inverted. (iii) At C: image at C, same size, real and inverted. (iv) Between C and F: image beyond C, enlarged, real and inverted. (v) Between P and F: image behind the mirror, enlarged, virtual and erect. Use: shaving mirrors (or dentists' mirrors), which give an enlarged, erect image of the face or of a tooth.
valuePoints: At infinity: at F, point-sized, real, inverted
Beyond C: between F and C, diminished, real, inverted
At C: at C, same size, real, inverted
Between C and F: beyond C, enlarged, real, inverted
Between P and F: behind mirror, enlarged, virtual, erect; used as shaving or dentist's mirror

rubric.label: At infinity
rubric.descriptor: Position, size, nature

rubric.label: Beyond C
rubric.descriptor: Position, size, nature

rubric.label: At C
rubric.descriptor: Position, size, nature

rubric.label: Between C and F
rubric.descriptor: Position, size, nature

rubric.label: Between P and F with use
rubric.descriptor: Behind mirror, enlarged, virtual, erect (½); shaving/dentist's mirror (½)

questions.stem: A convex lens has a power of +5 D. (a) Find its focal length. (b) An object 4 cm tall is placed 40 cm from the lens. Find the position, size and nature of the image. (c) The object is now moved to 10 cm from the lens. Find the new position, magnification and nature of the image.
questions.answer: (a) f = 1/P = 1/(+5 D) = +0.2 m = +20 cm. (b) u = −40 cm. Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, so 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/40 = 1/40, v = +40 cm (on the other side of the lens). m = v/u = 40/(−40) = −1, h′ = −4 cm: real, inverted, same size. (c) u = −10 cm: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20, v = −20 cm (on the same side as the object). m = v/u = (−20)/(−10) = +2, h′ = +8 cm: virtual, erect, magnified twice.
valuePoints: f = +20 cm
u = −40 cm → v = +40 cm, m = −1, h′ = −4 cm; real, inverted, same size
u = −10 cm → v = −20 cm, m = +2; virtual, erect, enlarged

rubric.label: Image position at 40 cm
rubric.descriptor: v = +40 cm using lens formula with signs

rubric.label: Size and nature at 40 cm
rubric.descriptor: h′ = −4 cm; real, inverted, same size

rubric.label: Image position at 10 cm
rubric.descriptor: v = −20 cm

rubric.label: Magnification and nature at 10 cm
rubric.descriptor: m = +2; virtual, erect, enlarged

questions.passage: A student looked up the absolute refractive index of some materials and noted: water 1.33, kerosene 1.44, crown glass 1.52 and diamond 2.42. She also learnt that kerosene, although it floats on water and has a lower mass density, is optically denser than water. In the laboratory she then sent a narrow beam of light obliquely from water into a block of crown glass kept in the water, and measured the angles of incidence and refraction at the surface where the light entered the glass. The speed of light in air is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: In which of the four materials does light travel fastest?
parts.answer: (d) — water has the lowest refractive index of the four, and speed = c/n is largest when n is smallest.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of light in diamond.
When the beam passes from water into the glass, does it bend towards or away from the normal? Explain, and say why kerosene is called optically denser than water.
parts.answer: Towards the normal: crown glass (1.52) has a larger refractive index than water (1.33), so light slows down on entering it and bends towards the normal. Kerosene is optically denser because its refractive index (1.44) is larger than that of water; optical density is not the same as mass density. (1 mark: towards the normal with reason; 1 mark: optical density judged by refractive index, not mass density)

questions.assertion: Stars twinkle, but planets do not.
questions.reason: Planets are much closer to the earth and are seen as extended sources, so the variations in light from their many point-sized sources average out to zero.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: a star is effectively a point source whose apparent position and brightness fluctuate because of atmospheric refraction, while for an extended planet the fluctuations cancel out.

questions.assertion: Myopia is corrected by using a convex lens of suitable power.
questions.reason: In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina.
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: A is false: myopia is corrected with a concave lens, which brings the image back on to the retina. R is true.

questions.stem: What is meant by the power of accommodation of the eye? What happens to the eye lens when we shift our gaze from a distant tree to a book held close to us?
questions.answer: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length so as to see both near and distant objects clearly is called accommodation. When looking at the nearby book, the ciliary muscles contract, the curvature of the eye lens increases and the lens becomes thicker, so its focal length decreases and the book is focused on the retina.
valuePoints: Accommodation: ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length
For the near book: ciliary muscles contract, lens thicker, focal length decreases

rubric.label: Definition
rubric.descriptor: Adjusting focal length to see near and far objects

rubric.label: Change for near object
rubric.descriptor: Ciliary muscles contract, lens thicker/more curved, focal length decreases

questions.stem: What is dispersion of light? Why does a glass prism split white light into a band of colours?
questions.answer: The splitting of white light into its component colours is called dispersion. Different colours of light bend through different angles as they pass through the prism — red bends the least and violet the most — so the colours emerge along different paths and become distinct, forming the spectrum VIBGYOR.
valuePoints: Dispersion = splitting of white light into its component colours
Different colours bend through different angles (red least, violet most) and emerge along different paths

rubric.label: Definition
rubric.descriptor: Splitting of white light into its colours

rubric.label: Reason
rubric.descriptor: Different colours bend by different amounts; red least, violet most

questions.stem: Give reasons: (a) 'Danger' signal lights are red in colour. (b) The sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes.
questions.answer: (a) Red light is scattered the least by fog or smoke, so a red signal can be seen in the same colour from a distance. (b) At very high altitudes there is hardly any air or fine particles to scatter sunlight, so scattering is not prominent; no scattered blue light reaches the eye and the sky looks dark.
valuePoints: Red is least scattered by fog/smoke, so it is visible from far
Little scattering at great heights, so the sky looks dark

rubric.label: Red danger signal
rubric.descriptor: Red least scattered, seen from a distance

rubric.label: Dark sky at altitude
rubric.descriptor: Scattering not prominent at such heights

questions.stem: A student cannot see objects beyond 2 m clearly. Name the defect of vision, give one possible cause of it, and find the nature and power of the lens needed to correct it.
questions.answer: The defect is myopia (near-sightedness): the far point is 2 m instead of infinity. Cause: excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. The corrective lens must form a virtual image of a distant object (u = −∞) at the far point, v = −2 m. 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/(−2 m) − 0, so f = −2 m. P = 1/f = −0.5 D: a concave (diverging) lens of power −0.5 D.
valuePoints: Myopia
Cause: excessive curvature of eye lens or elongated eyeball
Concave lens, f = −2 m, P = −0.5 D

rubric.label: Defect
rubric.descriptor: Myopia

rubric.label: Cause
rubric.descriptor: Excess curvature of lens or elongation of eyeball

rubric.label: Correcting lens
rubric.descriptor: Concave lens (½), P = −0.5 D (½)

questions.stem: The Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before it actually crosses the horizon at sunrise and about 2 minutes after it has crossed it at sunset. Explain this, and name one other effect seen at sunrise and sunset due to the same cause.
questions.answer: This is due to atmospheric refraction. When the Sun is just below the horizon, its light enters the earth's atmosphere, whose refractive index changes gradually, and is bent towards the normal. The light therefore reaches us from a direction slightly above the true position, so the Sun appears above the horizon about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and remains visible about 2 minutes after actual sunset. The apparent flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to atmospheric refraction.
valuePoints: Cause is atmospheric refraction
Light from Sun below horizon is bent towards the normal so the Sun appears raised above the horizon
Apparent flattening of the Sun's disc

rubric.label: Phenomenon
rubric.descriptor: Names atmospheric refraction

rubric.label: Explanation
rubric.descriptor: Bending of sunlight makes the apparent position higher than the actual one

rubric.label: Other effect
rubric.descriptor: Apparent flattening of the Sun's disc

questions.stem: Explain how a rainbow is formed. In which direction relative to the Sun would you look to see one, and where else can a rainbow be seen on a sunny day?
questions.answer: A rainbow is a natural spectrum caused by dispersion of sunlight by tiny water droplets in the atmosphere after a rain shower. Each droplet acts like a small prism: sunlight is refracted and dispersed on entering the drop, reflected internally inside it, and refracted again as it comes out, so different colours reach the observer's eye. A rainbow is always formed in the direction opposite to the Sun, so we must have the Sun behind us. It can also be seen through a waterfall or a water fountain on a sunny day, with the Sun behind the observer.
valuePoints: Water droplets act as prisms and disperse sunlight
Refraction and dispersion, internal reflection, refraction again
Seen opposite the Sun; also at a waterfall or fountain with Sun behind

rubric.label: Droplets as prisms
rubric.descriptor: Dispersion of sunlight by water droplets

rubric.label: Path in the drop
rubric.descriptor: Refraction with dispersion, internal reflection, refraction out

rubric.label: Direction and other places
rubric.descriptor: Opposite to the Sun (½); waterfall/fountain (½)

questions.stem: (a) Distinguish between myopia and hypermetropia in terms of what the person cannot see, where the image is formed, and two causes of each. (b) The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 50 cm. Find the power of the lens needed so that the person can read a book held at 25 cm. (c) What is presbyopia and how are bifocal lenses used?
questions.answer: (a) Myopia: distant objects are not seen clearly; the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; causes — excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. Hypermetropia: nearby objects are not seen clearly; light from a nearby object is focussed behind the retina; causes — focal length of the eye lens too long or eyeball too small. (b) The lens must form a virtual image at the near point of an object at 25 cm: u = −25 cm, v = −50 cm. 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/50 + 1/25 = 1/50, so f = +50 cm = +0.5 m and P = +2 D (a convex lens). (c) Presbyopia is the decrease of the power of accommodation with age, due to weakening of the ciliary muscles and reduced flexibility of the eye lens, so nearby objects are hard to see. A person with both myopia and hypermetropia uses bifocal lenses: the upper part is concave for distant vision and the lower part is convex for near vision.

questions.stem: Describe the function of each of the following parts of the human eye: cornea, iris, pupil, eye lens with ciliary muscles, and retina with optic nerve. What are the near point and the far point of a normal eye?
questions.answer: Cornea: a thin transparent membrane forming the bulge at the front of the eye through which light enters; most of the refraction occurs at its outer surface. Iris: a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil. Pupil: regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye. Eye lens with ciliary muscles: the lens provides the finer adjustment of focal length and forms an inverted real image on the retina; the ciliary muscles change its curvature. Retina and optic nerve: the retina has light-sensitive cells that are activated by light and generate electrical signals, which the optic nerves carry to the brain for interpretation. Near point (least distance of distinct vision) of a normal young adult eye is about 25 cm; the far point is infinity.

questions.passage: During a school trip to a hill forest, students noticed that early in the morning the sunlight coming through gaps in the dense canopy of trees looked like bright visible beams. Back in the laboratory, their teacher passed a narrow beam of light through a glass of salt solution and then through a glass of dilute milk; the path of the beam could be seen only in the milk. She explained that very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, while larger particles scatter longer wavelengths, and that red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times that of blue light.

parts.prompt: The visible beams of sunlight in the forest are an example of
parts.answer: (b) — tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light and make the path of the beam visible, which is the Tyndall effect.

parts.prompt: Why was the path of the beam not visible in the salt solution?
parts.answer: Salt solution is a true solution; its particles are too small to scatter light, so the path of the beam is not visible (it is visible in milk, a colloid, whose larger particles scatter light).

parts.prompt: Using the teacher's explanation, explain why the clear sky appears blue.
parts.answer: Air molecules and fine particles in the atmosphere are smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and they scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) much more strongly than longer ones (red, about 1.8 times longer). The scattered blue light enters our eyes from all directions, so the sky looks blue. (1 mark: fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths more; 1 mark: scattered blue light reaches the eye)

questions.stem: Describe how electricity is supplied and distributed in a house. In your answer, name the three wires and their usual colours, the potential difference of the supply, the path through the meter and the main switch, the two separate circuits and their ratings, and how appliances are connected. Explain what short-circuiting is and how the fuse protects the circuit.
questions.answer: Power reaches the house from the mains by overhead poles or underground cables. The live wire has red insulation and the neutral wire black insulation; the potential difference between them in India is 220 V. A third wire, the earth wire with green insulation, is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. At the meter-board the wires pass through a main fuse into the electricity meter, and through the main switch to the line wires of the house. Usually two separate circuits are used: a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances such as geysers and air coolers, and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans. Appliances are connected in parallel across the live and neutral wires, each with its own switch, so that each gets the same potential difference. Short-circuiting happens when the live and neutral wires come into direct contact (damaged insulation or a fault in the appliance), and the current rises abruptly. The fuse, placed in series, then heats up, melts and breaks the circuit, preventing damage to the wiring and appliances.

15 A circuit for high-power, 5 A for bulbs and fans

questions.stem: (a) Describe an activity to show that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, and how the direction of the force depends on the current and the field. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the displacement, and interchanging the poles (reversing the field) also reverses it; so the force depends on the directions of both the current and the field, and is perpendicular to both. (b) Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, the thumb points in the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor. (d) The proton beam is a current towards the north (middle finger north) and the force is towards the east (thumb east); the forefinger then points vertically upwards, so the field is directed upwards.

questions.stem: What are decomposers? Explain their role in an ecosystem and what would happen if they were absent.
questions.answer: Decomposers are microorganisms — bacteria and fungi — that break down the dead remains and waste products of organisms. They convert complex organic substances into simple inorganic substances that go into the soil and are used again by plants, so nutrients are recycled. Without them dead plants, animals and garbage would pile up, and the natural replenishment of the soil would not take place.
valuePoints: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi
They break complex organic matter into simple inorganic substances returned to the soil for plants
In their absence dead matter accumulates and soil is not replenished

questions.stem: (a) What is biological magnification? Explain how pesticides enter a food chain and why their concentration is highest in human beings. (b) Why can pesticide residues not always be removed from food? (c) Give two features of the flow of energy through the trophic levels of an ecosystem.
questions.answer: (a) Biological magnification is the progressive accumulation of harmful non-degradable chemicals at each trophic level of a food chain. Pesticides and other chemicals used to protect crops are washed into the soil or into water bodies. From the soil they are absorbed by plants along with water and minerals, and from water bodies they are taken up by aquatic plants and animals; this is how they enter the food chain. Because they are not degradable, they accumulate at each trophic level, and as human beings occupy the top level of any food chain, the maximum concentration builds up in our bodies. (b) The residues are present inside food grains, vegetables, fruits and meat, so they cannot always be removed by washing or other means. (c) Energy flow is unidirectional — energy passed to herbivores does not come back to the autotrophs; and the energy available diminishes progressively at each trophic level because of loss at each level.
valuePoints: Definition: accumulation of non-degradable chemicals increasing up the trophic levels
Pesticides reach soil and water, then plants and aquatic organisms
Not degradable, so they accumulate; humans at the top have the highest concentration
Residues are within the food, not removable by washing
Energy flow unidirectional; diminishes at each level

questions.stem: (a) Why are some substances biodegradable and others non-biodegradable? (b) Give two ways in which non-biodegradable wastes harm the environment. (c) If all the waste we generate were biodegradable, would it have no impact on the environment? Explain. (d) Suggest two ways in which you can help reduce the problem of waste disposal.
questions.answer: (a) Substances broken down by biological processes (the action of bacteria and other saprophytes through their enzymes) are biodegradable; enzymes are specific, and substances such as plastics for which no such enzymes exist are not broken down and are non-biodegradable. (b) They persist in the environment for a long time; they may harm various members of the ecosystem; they pile up as garbage and litter public places (any two). (c) No. Biodegradable waste still has an impact: large amounts of it pile up as garbage and take time to decompose, and untreated sewage and waste can pollute water bodies and soil; it must still be collected and treated. (d) Any two: separate biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste at home; use cloth bags instead of plastic bags; avoid disposable items; reuse and recycle materials; make compost from kitchen waste.
valuePoints: Biodegradability depends on whether microbial enzymes can break the substance down
Two harms of non-biodegradable waste
Biodegradable waste in large amounts still pollutes and must be managed
Two practical ways to reduce waste

questions.passage: A student preparing a class talk wrote these notes. The amount of ozone in the atmosphere began to drop sharply in the 1980s. The decrease has been linked to synthetic chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which are used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. Ozone high in the atmosphere protects living things from ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. In 1987 the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and it is now mandatory for manufacturing companies all over the world to make CFC-free refrigerators.

parts.prompt: Which of the following is linked to the depletion of the ozone layer?
parts.answer: (b) — CFCs, used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers, have been linked to the drop in ozone.

parts.prompt: Name one harmful effect on human beings of more ultraviolet radiation reaching the earth.
parts.answer: It is known to cause skin cancer in human beings.

parts.prompt: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern, and what steps have been taken to limit it?
parts.answer: The ozone layer shields the earth's surface from UV radiation, which is highly damaging to organisms, so its depletion would expose life to this radiation. Steps: the 1987 UNEP agreement froze CFC production at 1986 levels, and all manufacturers must now make CFC-free refrigerators. (1 mark: protective role against UV; 1 mark: the steps)
